extracted.intended_audience: Potential petitioners and their counsel (in-house counsel, IP litigators, and patent attorneys) considering or preparing IPRs/PGRs before the PTAB
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and procedural standards for preparing, filing, and litigating inter partes reviews (IPRs) and post-grant reviews (PGRs) before the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB), including eligibility, petition content, timing, burdens, and trial practice. Aimed at practitioners assessing whether and how to challenge patent validity before the PTAB.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and Purpose of IPRs and PGRs
rubrics_metrics.description: An inter partes review (IPR) or post-grant review (PGR) is a proceeding designed to allow a Petitioner to attack the validity of one or more claims of an issued patent. These proceedings are designed to provide a faster, cheaper alternative to district court litigation. IPRs and PGRs only examine validity and do not adjudicate infringement or award damages, injunctions, or other remedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use IPR/PGRs when the goal is to challenge patent validity quickly and cost-effectively; they do not resolve infringement or award relief beyond patentability determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences: Eligibility and Window of Opportunity (IPR vs PGR)
rubrics_metrics.description: For PGRs, only patents with at least one AIA claim (priority date on or after March 16, 2013) are eligible, and a PGR must be brought within nine months of issuance (or re-issuance). For IPRs, all patents are eligible and there is no general deadline to file, but if the patent has at least one AIA claim, one must wait to file a Petition until the later of nine months after issuance (or re-issuance) or termination of any PGR on the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check patent priority dates and issuance/re-issuance dates to determine whether to pursue PGR or IPR and to avoid premature filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible Grounds of Attack (IPR vs PGR)
rubrics_metrics.description: For IPRs, the only attacks allowed are anticipation (35 U.S.C. § 102) and obviousness (35 U.S.C. § 103) based upon patents and printed publications. For PGRs, in addition to anticipation and obviousness, one can also attack based on lack of written description (§ 112), indefiniteness (§ 112), lack of enablement (§ 112), and eligibility (§ 101).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the proceeding that permits the substantive grounds you intend to assert. Note eligibility challenges (§ 101) cannot be initially raised in IPR but may arise for proposed amended claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction: Prior District Court Civil Action
rubrics_metrics.description: If you (and any real party-in-interest) have previously filed a civil action in district court challenging the validity of the same patent, you cannot then file an IPR or PGR attacking that validity. The theory is an attacker should not get 'two bites at the [validity] apple.' However, filing a civil action for a declaratory judgment of noninfringement does not bar a concurrent or subsequent PTAB challenge; and filing a counterclaim for declaratory judgment of invalidity does not bar a subsequent IPR or PGR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide strategically whether to initiate validity challenges in district court or at the PTAB; consider timing and the one-year rules discussed below.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-Year Deadline When Served with Infringement Complaint
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have been served with a complaint for patent infringement in district court, you MUST file the petition within one year of service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the one-year clock as firm and allow extra time for unforeseen issues; use one year from service even if the complaint has defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition Thresholds for Institution (burden to show)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an IPR to be instituted, the Petition must demonstrate a reasonable likelihood that the Petitioner will prevail as to at least one of the claims challenged (may encompass a 50/50 chance). For a PGR to be instituted, the Petition must demonstrate that it is more likely than not that at least one of the claims challenged is unpatentable (greater than 50% chance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft petitions to meet the applicable statutory standard — IPR: reasonable likelihood; PGR: more likely than not. Focus on convincing the Board that at least one claim meets the institution threshold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of Proof at PTAB vs District Court
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden of proof in IPRs and PGRs is 'preponderance of the evidence' whereas the burden of proof in district court and before the ITC is 'clear and convincing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage the lighter PTAB burden when evaluating comparative strengths of forum selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Director and PTAB Discretion on Institution
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the Petition meets statutory thresholds, the Director (and PTAB) has discretion on whether to institute a trial. Factors include efficiency of the process, fundamental fairness for all parties, and whether the same or substantially the same prior art or arguments were previously presented to the Office (including previously-filed petitions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate and address discretionary denial bases — e.g., explain efficiency, distinguish prior presentations of the same art/arguments, and show fairness concerns favor institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who May File and Government Exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person who is not the owner of the patent may file an IPR or PGR. The U.S. Government is not a 'person' within the meaning of 35 U.S.C. § 311 and thus cannot bring an IPR or PGR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify petitioner status; corporate or related-party relationships can create real-party-in-interest issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity and Identification of Real Parties-in-Interest (RPI)
rubrics_metrics.description: No. The Petitioner and all real parties-in-interest must be identified. Failure to properly list all real parties-in-interest can be fatal to your attack.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct thorough investigation and disclosure of RPIs before filing; omissions can lead to invalidation of the proceeding or other severe consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition Scope and Filing Limits (one patent per petition; word limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Petition may only attack one patent. Petitions have word limits: 14,000 words for IPRs and 18,700 words for PGRs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure content to fit within word limits and challenge strategy to target one patent per petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required Contents of a Petition
rubrics_metrics.description: The Petition must set forth: the grounds for standing, the claim(s) attacked, the statutory grounds for the attack, how the claims are to be construed, and how/why the construed claim is unpatentable. The Petition must also identify the real parties-in-interest, related matters, lead and back-up counsel, and service information. The Petition is typically supported by one or more declarations of technical experts and supporting exhibits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure petitions include complete procedural and substantive components; include clear claim charts, claim constructions, and supporting expert declarations/exhibits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim Construction Standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent claims in IPRs and PGRs are construed using the same claim construction standard that would be used in a civil action in district court, including 'construing the claim in accordance with the ordinary and customary meaning of such claims as understood by one of ordinary skill in the art and the prosecution history pertaining to the patent.' 37 C.F.R. § 42.100(b); see Phillips v. AWH Corp.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Phillips/ordinary-and-customary-meaning standard in drafting claim construction arguments and connected invalidity analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition Filing Process and Procedural Compliance Review
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a Petition is filed, PTAB staff reviews the Petition for procedural compliance. If the Petition meets clerical criteria, PTAB issues a Notice of Being Accorded a Filing Date; if not, PTAB issues a Notice of deficiencies and sets a deadline for correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare filings to avoid clerical defects and be ready to respond promptly to deficiency notices to preserve filing dates and timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead Counsel Registration and Use of District Court Counsel
rubrics_metrics.description: Lead counsel in IPRs and PGRs must be registered to practice at the PTO. District court counsel who are not registered patent attorneys may serve as back-up counsel if admitted pro hac vice; PTAB generally permits such admission upon a showing of good cause (experience and familiarity with subject matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm lead counsel PTO registration early; arrange for registered backup or seek pro hac vice admission where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost and Fee Structure
rubrics_metrics.description: PTO filing fee for an IPR is currently $19,000 (for up to 20 claims) and $22,500 for the post-institution fee (for up to 20 claims), which must be paid at filing. PTO filing fee for a PGR is currently $20,000 (for up to 20 claims) and $27,500 for the post-institution fee (for up to 20 claims), which must be paid at filing. Filing fees alone are at least $41,500 for IPRs and $47,500 for PGRs. Additional claims can be challenged with payment of additional fees. If the petition is not instituted, the post-institution fee will be refunded upon request. Significant additional attorney and expert fees are typical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Budget for both PTO fees and substantial outside counsel/expert costs; account for additional-claim fees and possible refunds if not instituted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial-claim Attacks and Institution Consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: A Petitioner may attack some or all of the claims of the patent on one or more grounds of unpatentability. The PTAB will decide whether the Petition meets the burden for at least one challenged claim. If that burden is met and the PTAB exercises its discretion in favor of the Petitioner, the trial will be instituted on all of the challenged claims and all of the alleged grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if focused on a subset of claims, be prepared to litigate all challenged claims and grounds once institution occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeline of PTAB Proceedings (pre-institution and trial phases)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two major phases: a pre-institution phase (which lasts up to six months) and a post-institution or 'trial' phase (which lasts up to twelve months, absent special circumstances). The entire proceeding generally takes eighteen months or less from the time the Petition is accorded a filing date to issuance of the Final Written Decision. Specific clocks: Patent Owner has up to three months to file an optional Preliminary Response; PTAB then has up to three months to decide whether to institute; after institution the Patent Owner has three months to file a Response and Motion to Amend, Petitioner then has three months to Reply, etc., with final decision typically within three months of the oral hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan staffing and discovery with the PTAB’s compressed timeline in mind; calendar statutory and practice deadlines precisely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and Importance of Technical Experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Likely yes. Petitions are typically supported by at least one detailed declaration of a technical expert. The expert should have extensive experience in the subject matter of the challenged claims, be technically proficient, able to set forth opinions and bases, and able to withstand deposition. Commonly the same expert is used for the Petition and the Reply, though additional experts (e.g., economists) may be warranted to rebut Patent Owner evidence on objective indicia of non-obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retain qualified experts early; ensure declarations are detailed and defensible under cross-examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motions to Amend — Availability and Burdens
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent Owner may propose substitute claims (generally claim-for-claim). Motions to Amend are granted very rarely. Rules (as of Jan. 2021) state that the Patent Owner 'bears the burden of persuasion to show, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the motion to amend complies' with statutory/regulatory requirements; the Petitioner 'bears the burden of persuasion to show, by a preponderance of the evidence, that any proposed substitute claims are unpatentable.' The Board may, in the interests of justice, exercise discretion to grant or deny a motion to amend only for reasons supported by readily identifiable and persuasive evidence of record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate high bar for successful motions to amend; litigate amendment issues aggressively and develop record-based reasons for/against amendment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oral Hearing Preparation and Limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Oral Hearings are one of the few opportunities to interact with the APJ panel. Preparation is a must and requires in-depth familiarity with the record. APJ panels prepare extensively and know the record; litigants must be similarly prepared and able to respond to interrogation. Demonstrative exhibits are often submitted (cannot include new evidence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare demonstratives in advance, rehearse direct and cross Q&A, and ensure no new evidence is introduced at hearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final Written Decision Content and Timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Within three months of the Oral Hearing the panel issues its Final Written Decision, which addresses all bases and all claims raised in the Petition as well as patentability of any proposed amended claims. Final Written Decisions typically address claim construction (when necessary), weight given to experts' opinions, fact-findings regarding scope and content of the prior art, the Panel’s judgment on disputed evidence, and reasoning behind the Board’s conclusion as to patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop record evidence and expert testimony to support favorable fact-findings and to counter opposing expert weight arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rehearing Requests — Limitations and Requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A single request for rehearing may be filed within 30 days of entry of a final decision. Requests for rehearing rarely succeed. Any such motion must specifically identify all matters the movant believes the Board misapprehended or overlooked, and indicate where in the record each matter was previously addressed in a motion, opposition, or reply. 37 C.F.R. § 42.71(d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only seek rehearing when there is a clear record-based basis; precisely identify alleged misapprehensions and cite the record locations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to the Federal Circuit and Standard of Review
rubrics_metrics.description: A Petitioner may appeal to the Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit (must have standing). The Federal Circuit reviews the Board’s decision under the Administrative Procedure Act, which requires setting aside Board conclusions or findings that are 'arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise not in accordance with law,' or 'unsupported by substantial evidence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider appeal only when there are strong legal or substantial-evidence arguments; appellate review is for APA standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlements and PTAB Authority to Continue
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties may settle. The PTAB has the right to step into the shoes of the Petitioner and proceed with the patentability analysis. The earlier in the process a settlement occurs, the less likely the PTAB is to continue without both parties; the further along, the more likely the PTAB will finish its analysis and issue a Final Written Decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When negotiating settlement, consider PTAB’s authority to continue and how timing affects the likelihood of continued prosecution by the Board.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel Effects — Impact on District Court and PTO Proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Estoppel attaches once a Final Written Decision issues. A Petitioner cannot assert in district court any ground (invalidity argument) that was raised or reasonably could have been raised in the IPR or PGR. Similarly, the outcome may impact other proceedings at the PTO: a Petitioner (and any RPI and privy) is estopped from requesting or maintaining a proceeding in the PTO with respect to a claim for which a Final Written Decision has issued on any ground that was raised or reasonably could have been raised in the IPR or PGR. See 35 U.S.C §§ 315(e), 325(e); 37 C.F.R. § 42.73(d)(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze long-term litigation strategy and collateral estoppel consequences before filing or settling; preserve issues you want to keep available for other forums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery Scope and Standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery is permitted but limited compared to district court. Routine discovery includes: (1) production of any exhibit cited in a paper or testimony; (2) cross-examination of the other side’s declarants; and (3) relevant information inconsistent with a position advanced during the proceeding. Additional discovery: for IPRs, further discovery allowed if it furthers the 'interests of justice' (35 U.S.C. § 316(a)(5); 37 C.F.R. § 42.51(b)(2)); for PGRs, where 'good cause' is shown and limited to evidence directly related to factual assertions advanced by either party (35 U.S.C. § 326(a)(5); 37 C.F.R. § 42.224).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor discovery requests narrowly; be prepared to justify additional discovery under the narrower PTAB standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protective Order Default and Alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTAB has a default Protective Order. If either party wants a different Protective Order, there are procedures to get a different Order in place and the PTAB generally allows different Orders provided the need is shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use default order when appropriate; seek deviations with proper justification and follow PTAB procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistics and Strategic Considerations (why file)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents attacks before the PTAB have a high rate of success — approximately 60% of claims for which a trial has been instituted have been found unpatentable. Considering the high 'kill rate,' the speed, and the cost savings relative to district court proceedings, many find IPRs and PGRs attractive tools for removing patent obstacles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factor institution/outcome statistics into forum selection and client counseling, but assess the merits of the specific claims and prior art before filing.
